title: What you will be able to do
instruction: Press reveal to see each outcome for this lesson.

_items.text: Write with authority, aware of how your own stance shapes the argument you are making.

title: Authority is not the same as hiding
body: Many students assume that writing with authority means sounding neutral and keeping themselves out of the text entirely. The opposite is closer to the truth: authority comes from knowing your own stance, not concealing it.

title: Hyland's model of stance
body: Hyland's (2005) model names four devices writers use to show their stance: hedges (such as 'may suggest'), boosters (such as 'clearly shows'), attitude markers (showing surprise, importance, or agreement), and self-mention (naming yourself as the one making the claim). Marking your stance deliberately, through these four devices, is what turns a flat report into an authoritative argument, building on the synthesis work from earlier in this tier.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two drafts of the same dissertation chapter.

{{learner-a}} writes a chapter with no hedges, no boosters, and no self-mention, reporting findings as though no judgement went into selecting or weighing them.

{{learner-b}} writes the same chapter, marking a hedge where the evidence is thin, a booster where it is strong, and a sentence naming their own reading explicitly.

Both drafts covered the same findings. Only {{learner-b}}'s draft showed a stance the reader could actually see.

title: Why visible stance reads as more authoritative
body: A reader who can see where you hedge and where you push a claim harder trusts the places you push harder, precisely because you did not push everywhere equally. Authority comes from that visible, deliberate unevenness, not from a flat tone throughout.
Each device marks your stance in a different way. Select each tab to see an example.
instruction: Select each tab to see what each device does.

_items.title: Hedges
_items.body: Words like 'may suggest' or 'appears to' that mark where your claim is less certain. Example: 'This may suggest a wider pattern, though the sample is small.'

_items.title: Boosters
_items.body: Words like 'clearly' or 'demonstrates' that mark where your claim is strongly supported. Example: 'The results clearly demonstrate a consistent effect.'

_items.title: Attitude markers
_items.body: Words showing surprise, importance, or agreement. Example: 'Surprisingly, none of the three studies controlled for this factor.'

_items.title: Self-mention
_items.body: Naming yourself as the one making the claim. Example: 'I read this gap as significant, given what the other three studies found.'

title: Stance self-check
displayTitle: Before you submit a chapter or section
body: Use these questions to check your stance is visible, not hidden.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Did I hedge at least once, where the evidence is genuinely thin?
Did I boost at least once, where the evidence is genuinely strong?
Did I mark my own reading explicitly, rather than only reporting findings?
Would a reader be able to tell which claims I am most confident about?

title: Carrying this into your synthesis work
body: Go back to a section you have already synthesised from several sources. Mark one hedge, one booster, and one place for self-mention. The argument does not change; what changes is how visibly it is yours.

title: Your turn
instruction: This is for your own reflection; no right answers are expected.

_items.text: Find a sentence in your own writing with no hedge, booster, or self-mention at all. Which device would fit it best?
Is there a claim you have made that deserved a stronger booster than you gave it, or a hedge you left out?
